title: Business owners on financial thin ice
full_text:
Court actions by non big-four banks against distressed companies reached a record high in the September quarter, as more small business owners risk their homes and personal assets by seeking a “temporary lifeline” to keep their doors open.
According to the latest Alares Credit Risk Insights, there were more than 750 court actions by non big-four lenders with non-ADI (Authorised Deposit-taking Institution) lenders driving the increase, making up over 85 per cent of the total.
Insolvency and restructuring firm Jirsch Sutherland partner Malcolm Howell said more distressed small medium enterprises (SMEs) were turning to short-term finance to manage cash flow pressures, potentially putting their homes and personal assets at risk.
He said he and his colleagues have seen a sharp rise in struggling business owners taking on short-term loans with personal guarantees attached – often discovering the extent of their personal exposure only when the company enters liquidation.
“Directors aren’t taking on these loans for growth; they’re using them as a temporary lifeline to pay employees, suppliers and the ATO just to keep the doors open,” Mr Howell said.
“Short-term finance has always been around, but what’s changed is the number of owners turning to it when they’re already struggling, without realising what a personal guarantee can mean if the business fails.” Research released by ScotPac in June found 34 per cent of SMEs had sourced non-bank lending in the previous 12 months to support working capital.
Reserve Bank of Australia research also shows the non-bank share of SME lending has increased strongly since 2022, particularly for smaller loans.
The RBA noted that businesses may use higher-cost unsecured finance for relatively short periods to manage temporary cash flow issues.
Mr Howell said alternative and non-bank lenders were an increasingly visible source of fast finance for small businesses, with some promoting rapid or same-day approvals.
“That speed and accessibility can be attractive when a business is under cash flow pressure, but owners need to understand the cost, the terms and any personal guarantees they are signing,” he said. “These loans are often secured against the assets of the business, which can make it difficult to refinance or access further finance if it’s needed. It can leave an already struggling business with even fewer options.” It comes as insolvencies among small businesses are threatening to surge as falling house prices cuts the amount SME owners can borrow, when using their properties as collateral. Insolvency expert and BRI Ferrier principal Innis Cull said the combination of higher interest rates and a drop in property values could be the final straw for some struggling small businesses as the country heads towards a record year for company collapses. There were 5383 insolvencies in the September quarter, up 8.4 per cent from the same time last year, according to figures released by the Australian Securities & Investments Commission on Monday.
